mainTopic: How the wording of a food נדר decides its reach: prepared foods, fish and fish products, and dairy
overview: This amud teaches that the exact words of a נדר decide what becomes forbidden. If someone says 'from the pickled,' 'from the boiled,' 'from the roasted' or 'from the salted,' only the one food people usually mean is forbidden. If he says 'pickled that I taste' and so on, every food made that way is forbidden. רב אחא בריה דרב אויא asks about the Aramaic wordings דכביש and the others, and the question stays as תיבעי. The משנה then rules on vows against fish and fish products such as צחנה, טרית טרופה, ציר and מורייס. A ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says that דג means large fish and דגה means small fish. The גמרא tests this against פסוקים and concludes that in vows we follow לשון בני אדם, the way people talk. רבינא's question about the word ציחין stays unanswered. A new משנה begins on vows against milk, whey and cheese, and it starts the case of meat, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Vowing from pickled or boiled food
steps.stepSummary: The משנה contrasts two ways of wording a נדר. 'From the pickled' or 'from the boiled' forbids only the usual food: pickled vegetables or boiled meat. 'Pickled that I taste' or 'boiled that I taste' forbids every pickled or every boiled food.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNAH: If someone vows 'from the pickled,' he is forbidden only in pickled vegetables. If he says 'pickled that I taste,' he is forbidden in all pickled foods. If he vows 'from the boiled,' he is forbidden only in boiled meat. If he says 'boiled that I taste,' he is forbidden in all boiled foods.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives two pairs of cases, pickled and boiled. In each pair, a small change in wording changes how much food becomes forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a נדר we follow how people normally talk. People who say 'the pickled' usually mean pickled vegetables, and 'the boiled' usually means boiled meat, so only that food is forbidden. With the wording 'pickled that I taste,' he is speaking about the method of preparation itself, so every food made that way is included.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That I taste.' This wording makes the נדר cover the whole category

steps.confusionAlert: It looks backwards, but the shorter phrase 'from the pickled' forbids less. It points to the one familiar item. The phrase 'pickled that I taste' forbids more, because it describes a whole way of preparing food.
steps.whyThisMatters: This step sets up the basic rule of the whole section: a נדר is read by the speaker's exact wording and by everyday speech. The rest of the משנה and the גמרא's question are built on this rule.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
If he vowed: "From the pickled [food]"

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אָסוּר אֶלָּא מִן הַכָּבוּשׁ שֶׁל יָרָק.
phrases.english: he is forbidden only in pickled vegetables.
If he said: "Pickled [food] that I taste"
he is forbidden in all pickled foods.
If he vowed: "From the boiled [food]"

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ אָסוּר אֶלָּא מִן הַשָּׁלוּק שֶׁל בָּשָׂר.
phrases.english: he is forbidden only in boiled meat.
If he said: "Boiled [food] that I taste"
he is forbidden in all boiled foods.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ מִן הַכָּבוּשׁ אֵין אָסוּר אֶלָּא מִן הַכָּבוּשׁ שֶׁל יָרָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה about vows against foods described by how they are prepared.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'From the pickled' or 'from the boiled' forbids only the usual food: pickled vegetables or boiled meat. 'Pickled that I taste' or 'boiled that I taste' forbids every food prepared that way.

steps.title: Asking about the Aramaic wordings
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב אויא asks רב אשי about someone who vows using Aramaic forms: דכביש (that which is pickled), דשליק (boiled), דצלי (roasted) or דמליח (salted). Do these words point to the one usual food, or to the whole category?
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רב אחא בריה דרב אויא said to רב אשי: If someone said 'that which is pickled,' what is the law? 'That which is boiled,' what is the law? 'That which is roasted,' what is the law? 'That which is salted,' what is the law? What do these words mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about a new wording that the משנה did not discuss. It wants to know which of the משנה's two cases this wording is closer to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave two wordings with two results: only the usual food, or the whole category. The Aramaic form 'that which is pickled' does not clearly match either one. So רב אחא asks which way people mean it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
'Which way does it mean?' What does the wording point to?

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rav Avya, said to Rav Ashi:
If he said "that which is pickled," what [is the law]?
"That which is boiled," what [is the law]?
"That which is roasted," what [is the law]?
"That which is salted," what [is the law]?
Which way does it mean?
phrases.notes: He is asking whether these words point to the one usual food or to every food made that way.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the משנה's wording rule to a new set of Aramaic phrases.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'that which is pickled, boiled, roasted or salted' forbids only the usual food or every food prepared that way.

steps.title: The question stays open
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends with תיבעי: the question is not answered.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand as a question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רב אחא's question without an answer. The question is left unresolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source is found that tells us how people mean these Aramaic wordings. So the question stays open, and the law for these wordings is not decided here.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let it remain a question.' The question is left unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה gives two clear wordings: 'from the pickled' forbids only the usual food, and 'pickled that I taste' forbids the whole category. For the Aramaic wordings דכביש and the others, the גמרא leaves the question open (תיבעי).

phrases.english: Let it remain [a question].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from step 2 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The question stays open: we do not know whether the Aramaic wordings forbid only the usual food or the whole category.

steps.title: Vowing from roasted or salted food
steps.stepSummary: The משנה uses the same pattern for roasted and salted food. 'From the roasted' forbids only roasted meat (this is the view of רבי יהודה), and 'from the salted' forbids only salted fish. With the wording 'that I taste,' all roasted or all salted foods are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNAH: If someone vows 'from the roasted,' he is forbidden only in roasted meat; these are the words of רבי יהודה. If he says 'roasted that I taste,' he is forbidden in all roasted foods. If he vows 'from the salted,' he is forbidden only in salted fish. If he says 'salted that I taste,' he is forbidden in all salted foods.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds two more pairs, roasted and salted. They follow the same pattern as pickled and boiled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule has not changed. The usual 'roasted' food is meat and the usual 'salted' food is fish, so the 'from the' wording forbids only those. The 'that I taste' wording forbids the whole category.

keyTerms.meaning: 'These are the words of רבי יהודה.' The view belongs to רבי יהודה

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
If he vowed: "From the roasted [food]"

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אָסוּר אֶלָּא מִן הַצָּלִי שֶׁל בָּשָׂר,
phrases.english: he is forbidden only in roasted meat;
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
If he said: "Roasted [food] that I taste"
he is forbidden in all roasted foods.
If he vowed: "From the salted [food]"

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אָסוּר אֶלָּא מִן הַמָּלִיחַ שֶׁל דָּג.
phrases.english: he is forbidden only in salted fish.
If he said: "Salted [food] that I taste"
he is forbidden in all salted foods.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ מִן הַצָּלִי אֵין אָסוּר אֶלָּא מִן הַצָּלִי שֶׁל בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's pattern from step 1 with roasted and salted food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'From the roasted' forbids only roasted meat (רבי יהודה), and 'from the salted' forbids only salted fish. With 'that I taste,' all roasted or all salted foods are forbidden.

steps.title: Vowing from fish
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows 'fish' or 'fishes that I taste' is forbidden in every kind of fish: large or small, salted or unsalted, raw or cooked. He may still eat טרית טרופה (minced sardines) and ציר (fish brine).
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'fish' or 'fishes that I taste,' he is forbidden in them, whether large or small, salted or unsalted, raw or cooked. But he is permitted in minced sardines and in fish brine.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves on to a נדר against fish. It lists which foods count as fish and which do not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'fish' covers every kind of actual fish, no matter its size or how it was prepared. Minced sardines and brine are not called 'fish' in everyday speech, so they stay permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: The salty liquid that comes out of fish (brine)

phrases.english: If he said: "Fish [or] fishes that I taste"
he is forbidden in them,
whether large or small,
whether salted or unsalted,
whether raw or cooked,
but he is permitted in minced sardines and in fish brine.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּג דָּגִים שֶׁאֲנִי טוֹעֵם אָסוּר בָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from salted fish to a נדר against fish in general.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר against 'fish' forbids every kind of fish but does not forbid minced sardines or fish brine.

steps.title: Vowing from fish dishes: צחנה and minced sardines
steps.stepSummary: A נדר against צחנה also forbids minced sardines, but brine and מורייס stay permitted. A נדר against minced sardines also forbids brine and מורייס.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who vows from צחנה is forbidden in minced sardines, but permitted in fish brine and in מורייס. Someone who vows from minced sardines is forbidden in fish brine and in מורייס.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes with two fish-product cases. Each case shows what a נדר against one fish dish also includes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each fish product covers a different set of foods. A נדר against צחנה reaches minced sardines but not the liquids. A נדר against minced sardines also reaches the brine and the gravy that come out of them.

keyTerms.meaning: A dish of whole and chopped small fish

steps.whatToRemember: How far a food נדר reaches depends on what people normally call by that name. 'Fish' does not include brine. צחנה includes minced sardines. Minced sardines include brine and מורייס.

phrases.english: One who vows from tzachana
is forbidden in minced sardines,
but is permitted in fish brine and in fish gravy.
One who vows from minced sardines
is forbidden in fish brine and in fish gravy.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַצַּחֲנָה אָסוּר בְּטָרִית טְרוּפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues from fish to specific fish products and what each נדר includes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר against צחנה forbids minced sardines but not brine or מורייס. A נדר against minced sardines forbids brine and מורייס.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the words דג and דגה in a vow
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר teaches that a נדר on דג forbids large fish, a נדר on דגה forbids small fish, and a נדר on both forbids all fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: 'דג that I taste' forbids large fish and permits small fish. 'דגה that I taste' forbids small fish and permits large fish. 'דג דגה that I taste' forbids both large and small fish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה with a ברייתא that splits the two Hebrew words for fish into two different meanings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה (step 5) said that 'fish' forbids every kind of fish. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר adds a fine point: the exact word matters. דג means big fish and דגה means small fish, so you need both words to forbid everything.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה)
Fish; according to this ברייתא, a large fish
Fish; according to this ברייתא, small fish

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was taught in a ברייתא:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
'Fish (dag) that I taste' —
phrases.notes: This is short for a vow: 'fish is forbidden to me, so I will not taste it.'

phrases.english: he is forbidden in large fish and permitted in small fish.
'Fish (daga) that I taste' —
he is forbidden in small fish and permitted in large fish.
'Fish (dag), fish (daga) that I taste' —
he is forbidden in both large and small fish.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a detail to the משנה's ruling on vowing off fish
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דג forbids large fish only, דגה forbids small fish only, and both words together forbid all fish.

steps.title: How do we know דג means a large fish?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks אביי for the source that דג refers to a large fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: From where do we know that 'דג that I taste' means a large fish?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks for the source behind the ברייתא's claim that דג means a big fish. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave a ruling but no reason. רב פפא wants to know what tells us that דג is the word for big fish.

keyTerms.meaning: From where? How do we know?

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
From where do we know that 'fish (dag) that I taste'
refers to a large one?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the ברייתא's ruling
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that דג means a large fish

steps.title: Proof from יונה's great fish
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק calls the fish that swallowed יונה a 'דג גדול', a great fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And ה׳ prepared a great fish (דג) to swallow יונה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The proof is brought: the huge fish that swallowed יונה is called דג.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the word דג for an enormous fish. That suggests דג is the word for big fish.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (a פסוק is being quoted)

phrases.english: As it is written:
'And the Lord prepared a great fish (dag)
to swallow Jonah.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's question with a פסוק
steps.raayaSupportSource: יונה 2:1, where the great fish is called דג

steps.title: But the same fish is called דגה
steps.stepSummary: The very next פסוק calls the fish that held יונה a דגה, so דגה can also mean a large fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it written: 'And יונה prayed to ה׳ his God from the belly of the fish (דגה)'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof: the next פסוק calls the same big fish a דגה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If דגה can describe the huge fish of יונה, then דגה is not only for small fish. That would go against the ברייתא's split between the two words.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
'And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God
from the belly of the fish (daga)'!

steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that דגה means only small fish
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same big fish is called דגה in the next פסוק, so דגה can mean a large fish.

steps.title: Maybe it was a different, small fish
steps.stepSummary: The challenge is pushed off: maybe the big fish spat יונה out and a small fish swallowed him.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult: perhaps the large fish spat him out and a small fish swallowed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the challenge from step 10 by suggesting that two different fish were involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a second, smaller fish swallowed יונה, then the דגה in the second פסוק really was a small fish. So the יונה פסוקים do not prove that דגה can mean a big fish.

phrases.english: This is not difficult:
perhaps the large fish (dag) spat him out,
and a small fish swallowed him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns aside the challenge from step 10
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the challenge from יונה 2:2 (step 10); the proof from יונה 2:1 that דג means a large fish still stands
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The challenge assumes both פסוקים describe the same fish. They may describe two different fish, with the second one a small fish (דגה).

steps.title: The fish of the Nile all died
steps.stepSummary: A stronger challenge: the פסוק says 'the דגה in the river died', and surely the big fish died too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the difficulty is from this: 'And the fish (דגה) that was in the river died.' Did only the small fish die, and the large ones did not die?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the יונה challenge and brings a stronger one from the plague of blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here there is no way to say that only small fish were meant, because all the fish in the Nile died. So the תורה uses דגה for large fish too, which seems to go against the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (here it opens a stronger challenge)

phrases.english: Rather, the difficulty is from this:
'And the fish (daga) that was in the river died.'
Did the small ones die and the large ones not die?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected challenge with a stronger one
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that דגה means only small fish
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: All the fish in the Nile died, large ones included, yet the פסוק calls them דגה.

steps.title: In vows we follow how people talk
steps.stepSummary: In the תורה, דגה covers large and small fish. But in a נדר we go by everyday speech, where דגה means small fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, in the פסוק the word דגה means both large and small fish. But in vows, follow the language of people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that the תורה uses דגה for all fish. It explains that the ברייתא is based on how people speak, not on the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answers the challenge from the Nile. It also means the ברייתא never needed a פסוק to begin with. A נדר means whatever the words mean in daily speech, and people use דגה for small fish.

keyTerms.meaning: The way people talk; everyday speech

steps.whatToRemember: A נדר is understood by everyday language (לשון בני אדם), not by how the תורה uses a word. That is why דג and דגה can mean different things in a vow.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule of לשון בני אדם is a basic principle that runs through all of מסכת נדרים.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not conclude that the פסוקים prove the ברייתא. The גמרא ends up saying the פסוק uses דגה for every fish. The ברייתא's split comes only from how people talk.

phrases.english: Rather, the word 'fish (daga)' in the verse
means large fish and also means small fish,

phrases.aramaic: וּבִנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם.
phrases.english: but in vows, follow the language of people.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבִנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the Nile
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separates how the תורה uses a word from how people use it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's split between דג and דגה comes from the פסוקים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק uses דגה for all fish. The ברייתא follows everyday speech, where דגה means small fish.

steps.title: What if someone vows using the word ציחין?
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the משנה about צחנה, רבינא asks רב אשי about a vow using the word ציחין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who vows off צחנה...' רבינא said to רב אשי: If someone said, 'ציחין are forbidden to me', what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the line of the משנה about צחנה (step 6), and רבינא asks a new question about a similar word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ruled about צחנה. רבינא wants to know whether the similar word ציחין means the same thing in a נדר, which would give it the same law.

keyTerms.meaning: A word that sounds like צַחֲנָה. The question is whether it means the same thing in a vow
'They are hereby upon me' (forbidden to me), a formula for a vow

phrases.english: 'One who vows off tzaḥana', etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the line of the משנה from step 6, and the question below is about it.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
If someone said, 'Tziḥin are hereby forbidden to me', what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַצַּחֲנָה כּוּ׳. אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the דג/דגה topic and goes back to the next line of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a vow on ציחין has the same law as a vow on צחנה

steps.title: The question is left open
steps.stepSummary: רבינא's question about ציחין is not answered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the question with תיבעי, which means no answer is found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is added to settle whether ציחין equals צחנה. The question stays open, just like the question about pickled, boiled, roasted and salted in step 3.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unanswered

phrases.english: Let the question stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רבינא's question without an answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether a vow on ציחין has the law of צחנה is left unresolved.

steps.title: Vowing off milk or whey
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows off milk may still have whey (קום), but רבי יוסי forbids it. Someone who vows off whey may still have milk.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If a person vows not to have milk, he is allowed to have whey. רבי יוסי says he is forbidden. If he vows not to have whey, he is allowed to have milk.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It rules on whether a vow against milk also covers whey, and the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion treats whey as something separate from milk, so a vow against milk does not reach it. רבי יוסי forbids whey, since it comes from milk. In the reverse case, a vow against whey, no one disagrees: milk stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה.' It marks the start of a new משנה.
One who makes a vow (here, a vow to forbid a food to himself)
Whey, the liquid left over when milk is made into cheese

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי argues only about the first case (vowing off milk). In the reverse case (vowing off whey), milk is permitted and no one disagrees.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who vows off milk
is permitted to have whey,
phrases.notes: Whey is the watery liquid that separates out when milk is turned into cheese.

phrases.english: but Rabbi Yosei forbids it.
If he vowed off whey, he is permitted to have milk.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הֶחָלָב מוּתָּר בַּקּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the unanswered question about ציחין in step 15, a new משנה begins with a fresh set of food-vow cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow against milk does not forbid whey (רבי יוסי forbids it). A vow against whey does not forbid milk.

steps.title: Abba Shaul on vowing off cheese
steps.stepSummary: אבא שאול rules that someone who vows off cheese is forbidden every kind of cheese, salted or unsalted.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבא שאול says: If a person vows not to have cheese, he is forbidden to eat it, whether it is salted or unsalted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings אבא שאול's rule about a vow against cheese.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think a vow against 'cheese' covers only the most common type. אבא שאול teaches that the word covers both salted and unsalted cheese, so both are forbidden.

phrases.english: Abba Shaul says:
One who vows off cheese
is forbidden to eat it,
whether it is salted or unsalted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּא שָׁאוּל אוֹמֵר הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַגְּבִינָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה moves from milk and whey to another dairy food, cheese.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow against cheese forbids all cheese, salted and unsalted alike.

steps.title: The case of vowing off meat begins
steps.stepSummary: The משנה begins a new case about someone who vows off meat. The ruling continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person vows not to have meat...
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is setting up its next case, a vow against meat. The ruling itself comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line only names the case. Like the milk case, it will ask which foods related to meat are also covered by the vow.

phrases.english: One who vows off meat

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה moves on from dairy foods to a new food, meat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case of a vow against meat is introduced. Its ruling continues in the following text.
